business-narrative.name: Business Narrative
business-narrative.summary: Tell a business strategy or solution as a story: setting, challenge, tension, hero, plan, outcome. Useful for internal alignment decks, town halls, and any audience that responds better to story shape than to bullet lists.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Engage the audience and set expectations for the next twenty minutes. Tell them you're going to tell them a story — and then start telling it. Avoid a separate agenda slide; the introduction is the first scene.

beats.name: Setting
beats.description: Establish the world the story takes place in: the team, the market, the moment. Just enough context that the challenge will feel meaningful when it arrives.

beats.name: Challenge
beats.description: Identify the issue at hand. Concrete, specific, attributable. The challenge is the inciting incident — the thing that pulled the rest of the story into motion.

beats.name: Tension
beats.description: Raise the stakes. What happens if the challenge isn't met? Quantify the cost, name the people affected, surface the trade-offs that make the choice hard. Tension is what makes the audience lean in.

beats.name: Solution
beats.description: Reveal the strategy or hero of the story. Lead with what changes for the audience or customer when the solution is in place. This is the turn from problem to promise.

beats.name: Implementation
beats.description: Describe the path to success. Phases, owners, milestones, key bets. Show the audience that the solution has weight behind it — not just intent.

beats.name: Recap
beats.description: Bring the audience back to the surface with a clear summary of what was said and decided. Echo the language from the opening so the story feels closed.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Reinforce the key message and the call to action. End on the line you most want repeated in tomorrow's hallway conversations.
beats.instructions: Reinforce takeaways and call to action

all-hands.name: All Hands
all-hands.summary: The full company — mixed roles, mixed seniority, looking for context, signal, and inclusion.
all-hands.description: An all-hands audience spans the whole company. Frame the period in terms anyone can grasp: what we did, what mattered, and what's next. Highlight people and teams; surface successes and challenges; close on a forward-looking note. Avoid lapsing into function-specific jargon.

persuade.name: Persuade
persuade.summary: Change belief or win support for a specific argument, idea, or recommendation.
persuade.description: Use when the audience may be skeptical or undecided. Build a crisp thesis, support it with evidence, address objections, and end with a clear action.
persuade.outcome: The audience accepts the argument or supports the recommendation.

persuasive.name: Persuasive
persuasive.summary: Argument-led voice for sales, fundraising, and recommendation-driven decks.
persuasive.description: Frame every section as an argument that builds toward an ask. Surface objections, answer them, and pair claims with the strongest available proof. Read more like a memo than a report.
voiceCues: Lead each section with the claim it's making.
Surface the strongest counter-argument and address it.
Pair every claim with proof — customer, benchmark, or analyst.
End on a clear ask with named owner and date.
avoid: Symmetrical 'on one hand / on the other' framing without a verdict.
Information for its own sake — every chart should advance the argument.
Passive endings without a clear ask.
samplePhrases: Adopting our runtime cuts inference latency 8× while preserving accuracy.
The most common objection — 'we'll be locked in' — is addressed by our open OPF spec.
We're asking for a $30M Series B to ship into the enterprise tier.

bold.name: Bold
bold.description: A vibrant, high-energy theme with bold colors and a dynamic, attention-grabbing style. Great for presentations that need to stand out.

steel-blue.name: Steel Blue
steel-blue.summary: Cool steel blues for credible, data-forward presentations.
steel-blue.description: A steel-blue palette that combines credibility, precision, and calm. Useful for analysis-heavy decks.

burnt-orange.name: Burnt Orange
burnt-orange.summary: Warm orange and red accents for energetic commercial decks.
burnt-orange.description: A warm, high-contrast palette built around burnt orange, red, navy, and gold. It feels active without losing structure.

noto-sans.name: Noto Sans
noto-sans.description: Noto Sans is a sans serif OPF font scheme for complex script presentations, using Noto Sans for both headings and body text.

impact.name: Impact
impact.description: Impact is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Impact for headings with Grandview for body text.

title-subtitle.name: Title Subtitle
title-subtitle.summary: Reach for it when a headline needs one supporting line, as on a cover or a section opener.
title-subtitle.description: A title with a subtitle beneath it. Use it for the cover slide, for section openers, or for a closing slide with a headline and a short follow-up line.

text-2x.name: Text 2x
text-2x.summary: Reach for it when two blocks of prose sit side by side, such as a before and an after or a pro and a con.
text-2x.description: A title above two text blocks in a row. Use it to pair two explanations, set a problem next to its answer, or compare two options in sentences.

chart-2x.name: Chart 2x
chart-2x.summary: Reach for it when two charts are read together, each with its own note.
chart-2x.description: A title above two charts, each followed by a text block, in two columns. Use it to compare two series, two periods or two segments side by side.

list-5x.name: List 5x
list-5x.summary: Reach for it when five groups of points need parallel lists on one slide.
list-5x.description: A title above five lists in a three-column grid. Use it for five categories, stages or capabilities when each has only a few short bullets.
